karl.rizom.ai.response:
I find no passage in these sections that gives a direct rule for what a community should remember or forget. I can offer only a limited inference from what they do say.

History is not a store of fixed lessons or purposes: each generation inherits conditions from those before it, carries on activity under altered circumstances, and changes those conditions in turn. I write that history is “die Aufeinanderfolge der einzelnen Generationen,” each of which “die ihr von allen vorhergegangenen übermachten Materiale, Kapitalien, Produkionskräfte exploitiert” (*The German Ideology*, “Über die Produktion des Bewußtseins,” Ideologie, 44).

So a community should remember the material conditions and inherited relations that shape its life—and how people have acted upon and altered them. It should not mistake those inherited conditions for an eternal order or imagine that earlier generations made them for the sake of ours: “ohne indes sich einzubilden, es sei der Plan oder die Bestimmung der bisherigen Generationen gewesen, ihnen Material zu liefern” (*The German Ideology*, “Kommunismus. – Produktion der Verkehrsform selbst,” Ideologie, 70).

That is not a doctrine of collective forgetting. These passages say nothing specific about what a community ought to erase from memory; I will not supply an answer they do not contain.

friedrich.rizom.ai.response:
I would not prescribe one common storehouse of memories for every community. The past should be kept insofar as it serves life—and judged when it becomes a burden.

A community may remember what gives it roots: I call history “dem Bewahrenden und Verehrenden” when it lovingly tends what formed it, and thereby preserves “die Bedingungen, unter denen er entstanden ist, für solche … welche nach ihm entstehen sollen” (*On the Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life*, HL-3). But reverence must not turn age into an unquestionable claim: antiquarian history can “den kräftigen Entschluss zum Neuen” hinder and paralyze those who act (HL-3).

It should forget what it cannot carry without being crushed by it. “Das Vergangene vergessen werden muss, wenn es nicht zum Todtengräber des Gegenwärtigen werden soll,” I write; health depends on knowing “zur rechten Zeit zu vergessen” as well as remembering (*On the Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life*, HL-1). Forgetting is not simply weakness: it is “eine Thürwärterin” that makes room for “Ruhe” and “Neues” (*On the Genealogy of Morality*, GM-II-1).

Yet forgetting must not shield the past from judgment. At times, a community must “eine Vergangenheit zu zerbrechen und aufzulösen, um leben zu können”; the critical use of history serves life by bringing inherited things before judgment (*On the Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life*, HL-3).

So: remember what nourishes continuity and future life; forget what has become a dead weight; and critically break with what must be overcome. The measure is not memory for its own sake, but whether memory and forgetting leave a people able to live and create (HL-1; HL-3; GM-II-1).

sigmund.rizom.ai.response:
I find no rule in my works prescribing what a community ought to remember or forget. I can offer a caution, not a social programme: forgetting may serve an unacknowledged wish to avoid what is painful, and a people’s traditions may bear the mark of that wish.

I wrote: „Daß man bei der Entstehung der Traditionen und der Sagengeschichte eines Volkes einem solchen Motiv, das dem Nationalgefühl Peinliche aus der Erinnerung auszumerzen, Rechnung tragen muß, wird allgemein zugestanden.“ I add that a closer inquiry might show an analogy between the formation of national traditions and individual childhood memories. (*Zur Psychopathologie des Alltagslebens*, **GW IV, 162**.)

So I would not advise a community simply to preserve everything or to erase what wounds it. I would ask it to examine what its remembering and forgetting conceal—especially when an account leaves out what is painful or inconvenient. That is an inference from my account of motivated forgetting, not a prescription I set down for communities. (*Zur Psychopathologie des Alltagslebens*, **GW IV, 162**.)
